passage:
Dear Yamini Bua,
I wanted to thank you for Sunday lunch.
Since I was twelve, the family has had a nickname for me that I won't write here. This year, after a term of hostel food and football, everyone suddenly said, "Wah, so slim now, finally handsome!" I know they meant it kindly. But I realised the praise and the teasing were the same thing: both about my body, both telling me that's what counts. Now I feel every eye on my plate. If I take a second roti, I wait for someone to say something.
When Chachi started on my waist again, you said, "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?" The whole table moved on to exams.
Could you keep doing that? I think the others listen to you.
With love,
Vishal

qa.q: What did Yamini Bua ask Vishal at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: "Vishal, you've been playing so much football, are you sleeping enough?"

qa.q: What does Vishal worry about when taking a second roti?
qa.a: Vishal feels anxious and watched, expecting someone to comment on the plate.

qa.q: Which choice by Yamini Bua shifted the table, and why did it work?
qa.a: Yamini Bua turned the talk from Vishal's waist to football and sleep, focusing on health rather than looks, so the table moved on.

qa.q: Why might Chachi think those comments are harmless?
qa.a: Chachi probably means them as kindness or praise, and doesn't see that they make Vishal feel watched and valued only for looks.

grounding: It shows a young adult who, teased and then praised for their body, learns that looks are what count and feels watched at meals, until talk about health shifts the mood.

passage: People think compliments can't hurt. I'm Preeti, and I'm speaking at this wellness evening because of our college canteen. At school they called me names for being tall and bony. Then in college the same body got praise: "You should model." "Don't ever gain weight." Different words, same message: my body was the most interesting thing about me. I started to feel eyes on me at every meal. If I ate a samosa, someone said, "Careful!" If I skipped one, someone said, "Wow, discipline." So I stopped eating in the canteen at all. My roommate Pooja noticed. She didn't make a speech. One day she just said at our table, "New rule: no body talk while we eat. Tell me about your day instead." People laughed, and then they actually did it. It sounds small. It let me eat lunch again.

qa.q: What was Pooja's new rule at the table?
qa.a: No body talk while we eat.

qa.q: Why did Preeti feel watched at every meal?
qa.a: Both eating and skipping food drew comments, so Preeti felt self-conscious and judged over every food choice.

qa.q: What made Pooja's choice at the table effective?
qa.a: It was simple and friendly, swapping body talk for "Tell me about your day", so people could change the habit without feeling scolded.

qa.q: How might the people who said "You should model" see their own words?
qa.a: They probably thought they were giving compliments, not realising the praise taught Preeti that looks were Preeti's value.

grounding: It shows how teasing and praise about a body both teach that appearance is value and make meals feel watched, and how a roommate's kind table rule changes the climate.

passage: At her cousin's wedding in their small town, Rehana, twenty, heard it within minutes. "Arre, Rehana, you've become so healthy!" said one aunty. Another said, "No, no, she's looking slim now, very nice." At the lunch table, she felt every eye on her plate. She took a small spoon of biryani and pushed it around. Her cousin Asif noticed. He sat next to her and turned to the aunties. "Rehana's college project won a district prize. Tell them, Rehana." The aunties turned, surprised. Rehana explained her water-harvesting model, and for once they listened. Asif murmured, "Let's talk about what you do, not how you look." Rehana finally ate her biryani properly.

qa.q: What did Rehana's college project win?
qa.a: It won a district prize.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel at the lunch table?
qa.a: She felt watched and self-conscious, as if every eye was on her plate.

qa.q: What did Asif do that changed the climate?
qa.a: He steered the conversation from Rehana's body to her achievements, and reminded her to value what she does over how she looks.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Rehana after hearing about the project?
qa.a: They may see her as talented and interesting, not just as a body to comment on.

grounding: Shows a young adult teased and praised for her body who feels watched at meals, and a cousin whose kindness shifts talk from looks to achievement.

passage: At the rowing club in Stockholm, Ingrid, nineteen, had heard it all season. "You're getting so skinny, looking great!" "Careful, don't get bulky." Every comment made her more aware of her plate in the canteen, as if the whole team was counting. She started eating alone in the changing room. Their coach, Anders, noticed. At the next meeting he said, "From now on, no comments about anyone's body in this club, good or bad. We talk about strength, recovery and how we feel." Some rowers rolled their eyes, but it stuck. The next week, someone told Ingrid, "Your start was so powerful today." She smiled, and sat with the team at lunch.

qa.q: Where had Ingrid started eating?
qa.a: In the changing room, alone.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel after the comments about her body?
qa.a: She felt watched and self-conscious, as if the team were counting what she ate.

qa.q: What change did Anders make, and why did it help?
qa.a: He banned body comments and shifted talk to strength and health, which made the club feel safer for Ingrid.

qa.q: How might the other rowers experience the new rule?
qa.a: Some found it odd at first, but they may come to feel more relaxed too, with the focus on performance and wellbeing.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels watched at meals after body comments, and a coach who shifts the climate to kindness and health.

passage: In the engineering hostel mess, the boys had always called Mridul "Motu." Then over the summer he lost weight, and now they said, "Wah, Mridul, looking hot!" Both felt the same to him. At every meal he felt watched; if he took seconds, someone joked. He started skipping dinner and eating biscuits in his room. His roommate Uday noticed. At the table one night, when someone started, "Mridul's so fit now—" Uday cut in. "Can we drop the body talk? Mridul scored the winning goal on Sunday, talk about that." The table laughed and moved on. Later Uday said quietly, "You don't owe anyone a look. Come to dinner." Mridul came.

qa.q: What nickname did the boys use for Mridul before?
qa.a: They called him "Motu."

qa.q: How did Mridul feel at meals in the mess?
qa.a: He felt watched and uncomfortable, so he began skipping dinner and eating biscuits alone.

qa.q: What did Uday do that changed the climate at the table?
qa.a: He asked everyone to drop the body talk and turned the conversation to Mridul's winning goal.

qa.q: How might Uday feel when Mridul comes to dinner?
qa.a: Uday may feel glad and relieved that his friend feels safe enough to eat with everyone again.

grounding: Shows a young adult teased and then praised for his body, who feels watched at meals, and a friend who changes the climate with kindness.

passage:
Dear Payal Didi,
I wanted to say thank you for Sunday.
You know how every family lunch goes. Chachi says I've "grown healthy". Mama's friend praises me when I look thinner. Someone always watches what's on my plate. For years I've felt eyes on me at every meal. I started thinking my looks were the only thing people noticed.
On Sunday, when Chachi started again, you said, "Arohi just topped her engineering exam. Let's talk about that." And later, "We don't comment on anyone's body at this table. Only on how the food tastes."
Everyone laughed a bit awkwardly. But nobody watched my plate for the rest of the lunch. I ate without thinking about it for the first time in ages.
You made the whole table kinder. I won't forget it.
Love,
Arohi

qa.q: What did Payal Didi say Arohi had just done?
qa.a: Topped the engineering exam.

qa.q: How has Arohi felt at family meals for years?
qa.a: Arohi has felt watched and self-conscious, believing appearance was the only thing people valued.

qa.q: What changed the climate at the table?
qa.a: Payal Didi's kindness in shifting the talk to Arohi's achievement and setting a rule against body comments.

qa.q: How might Chachi have felt when Payal Didi spoke up?
qa.a: Chachi may have felt a little embarrassed or caught out, even if the comments were meant kindly.

grounding: Arohi, used to teasing and praise about appearance and feeling watched at meals, finds that a cousin's kindness and talk away from looks change the climate.
